## Learning outcomes

By the end of this part, you should be able to:

- Direct Claude Code to build a CMS-backed shop where the owner edits the product catalogue through an admin panel, with changes going live and no redeploy
- Wire up Stripe's hosted Checkout in the sandbox and prove that an order is marked paid only on a verified webhook, never because the customer reached the thank-you page
- Deploy the finished shop to a live URL, keeping every secret in environment variables rather than in the repository

<br>

---

<br>

## Overview

This project combines the sprint's work in one shop: a **CMS** (a login-protected admin panel where an owner edits content) from the CMS and payments lesson provides a catalogue that changes with no redeploy, **Stripe Checkout** from the same lesson handles the payment, and **Vercel** puts the shop live at a public URL.

A fuller production setup is not required here. Separate development and production databases are an optional task for anyone who wants the realistic version. One Supabase project and one deployment are enough for this project.

Only the money is fake: the shop runs in Stripe's sandbox with test keys, so no real card is ever charged and you never have to activate a Stripe account. Everything else is real: content editing, checkout, webhook payment confirmation, and deployment.

#### Topics

- Building a CMS-backed product catalogue an owner edits through an admin panel
- Stripe hosted Checkout in the sandbox, with the webhook as the only trustworthy payment signal
- Deploying the shop to Vercel, with the database connection string and the Stripe keys held in environment variables
- Optional extra: separate development and production databases

## Task description

You are building and shipping your own online shop. By default, build a small shop with a handful of products an owner can edit and a checkout that takes payment in Stripe's sandbox. The shop is yours to name and design. What it sells is up to you: a print shop, a coffee subscription, a set of houseplants, a page of merch. Keep the catalogue small, three or four products is plenty, so every step is easy to check.

**The idea is yours, as long as it keeps both halves.** You may replace the shop with your own product idea, provided it still uses a CMS with owner-editable content through an admin panel **and** takes a payment through Stripe Checkout. If it drops either half, it is not this project.

Here are four alternatives that need both a CMS and a payment. These are starting points, not the full list.

- **A paid digital-download store.** The owner uploads and prices digital goods through the admin panel (design presets, an e-book, print files). A customer pays through Stripe Checkout and gets access to the download. The catalogue is the CMS; the download unlocks on a verified payment.
- **A bookable paid service.** The owner edits the service details, dates, and prices in the admin panel (a workshop, a consultation, a class). A customer pays to book a slot through Stripe Checkout. The listings are the CMS; the booking is the payment.
- **A membership or supporter site.** The owner edits the members-only content and the price of access in the admin panel. Paying through Stripe Checkout unlocks that content for the customer. The content is the CMS; the unlock is the payment.
- **A ticketed event page.** The owner edits event details, dates, and ticket prices in the admin panel. A customer buys a ticket through Stripe Checkout. The event listings are the CMS; the ticket sale is the payment.

Whatever you choose, describe it clearly in `CLAUDE.md` so the agent (and your reviewer) knows what you are building and can see that it needs both a CMS and a payment.

## Task requirements

#### The exact task requirements are as follows

1. **A self-chosen shop, or an approved alternative, described in `CLAUDE.md`.** The default is a small shop with a few products. If you pick an alternative, it must still have owner-editable content through an admin panel and take a payment through Stripe Checkout. Describe what you are building, in plain language, at the top of `CLAUDE.md`.

2. **Both agent skills installed before you build.** Install the Payload skills and the Stripe plugin so the agent works from current, official guidance rather than its training data. Run both from inside your project folder:

```bash
npx skills add payloadcms/skills
```

```bash
claude plugin install stripe@claude-plugins-official
```

3. **A Payload CMS with an owner-editable catalogue.** Payload installs inside your Next.js app with a Products collection (or the equivalent for your idea), each item carrying at least a name, a price, a short description, and a photo uploaded through the admin panel. The access rule is: anyone can view products, only a logged-in admin can create, edit, or delete them. Prove it by editing a product in the admin panel and seeing the change live on the site with no redeploy. Describe the collection to the agent as behaviour, not code:

```text
Add a Products collection to the shop. Each product needs a name, a price, a
short description, and a single photo uploaded through the admin panel. Anyone
visiting the site can view products, but only a logged-in admin can create,
edit, or delete them.
```

4. **Stripe hosted Checkout in the sandbox, with a success and a decline both tested.** Using test keys only (`sk_test_` and `pk_test_`), complete a successful test purchase with the success card, then confirm the app handles a declined card gracefully without marking anything paid:

```text
4242 4242 4242 4242
```

```text
4000 0000 0000 0002
```

Use any future expiry date and any three-digit security code. Everything stays in test mode: no real money moves and no account activation is needed.

5. **Orders recorded as paid only on a verified webhook.** The order is marked paid when Stripe's own confirmation arrives at your app's server and the app verifies that it came from Stripe, never because the customer reached the thank-you page. Direct the agent to keep the two jobs separate:

```text
When a customer completes payment, Stripe will notify my app's server directly.
Only record the order as paid when that confirmation arrives from Stripe and is
verified as genuine, never just because the customer reached the thank-you page.
```

6. **A deployed, live shop with secrets kept out of the repository.** The shop is deployed to Vercel and reachable at a public URL your reviewer can open. The database connection string and your Stripe test keys live in Vercel's environment variables, never in the repository. One Supabase project is all you need: splitting development and production is an optional task.

## Optional tasks

Complete at least one optional task.

#### Easy

- **Order confirmation page.** After a successful payment, show the customer a confirmation page listing what they bought. Ask the agent: "After a successful payment, show a confirmation page that lists the product the customer just bought and confirms the order is paid."
- **A second Payload collection.** Add a collection a non-technical owner can edit without touching code, such as an About page or a list of FAQs. Confirm you can edit it in the admin panel and see the change live with no redeploy.
- **Sold-out state from the admin panel.** Let the owner mark a product as out of stock in the admin panel, and have the public site show it as sold out and refuse checkout for it.

#### Medium

- **An Orders collection in Payload.** Record each paid order as a row in an Orders collection so the owner can see paid orders in the admin panel. The order is only written when the webhook confirms payment.
- **A custom domain on production.** Register a domain and connect it to your production deployment, so the live shop is reachable at your own name over `https://`.
- **Instant-rollback rehearsal.** Make a trivial change that visibly breaks the live site, deploy it, then use Vercel's instant rollback to point the live site back at the last good deployment. Confirm the site is healthy again.
- **Separate development and production databases.** Create a second Supabase project so your local work never touches the live database, and scope each connection string to the right environment in Vercel.

#### Hard

- **A scheduled health check.** Set up a scheduled agent or a scheduled job on GitHub that runs once a day, checks the live shop is up and that products load, and tells you if something is wrong.
- **A written go-live plan.** Work through Stripe's go-live checklist and write up, without executing, exactly what would change to take real payments: activating the account, swapping test keys for live keys, registering a live webhook with its new signing secret, and recreating products and prices in live mode. Keep everything in the sandbox.
- **A documented migration flow.** Set up Supabase branching, or write up a migration flow of your own that would carry a database change from a development database to the live one, tested before it reaches live.
- **The full sandbox-to-production pipeline.** Build the pipeline from the production systems lesson: merging a pull request into `main` deploys a sandbox preview, and merging `main` into a separate `production` branch deploys the live site. Switch Vercel's own automatic deploys off so the workflow is the only thing that ships, and keep the three deployment secrets (`VERCEL_TOKEN`, `VERCEL_ORG_ID`, `VERCEL_PROJECT_ID`) in GitHub's encrypted Actions secrets rather than in the repository.

## Evaluation criteria

1. The shop works end to end. The owner edits a product in the admin panel and the change appears live with no redeploy, and a sandbox test purchase completes with the order marked paid only via the verified webhook. The student can complete a purchase with the success card in front of the reviewer and show that a declined card leaves nothing marked paid.
   Weight: 3

2. The shop is deployed and live. It is reachable at a public URL the reviewer can open, deployed to Vercel from the student's own repository.
   Weight: 3

3. Keys and environments are handled safely. The database connection string and the Stripe keys are set as environment variables in Vercel and never committed to the repository. Everything stays in Stripe's sandbox with test keys (`sk_test_` and `pk_test_`), with no real account activation and no real card. A single Supabase project is expected here; separate development and production projects are an optional task.
   Weight: 2

4. The project was built the sprint's way and documented: both agent skills installed before building, and a `README.md` covering what the shop sells, how the owner edits content, and how to run it locally.
   Weight: 1

5. At least one optional task was delivered and can be demonstrated in the running app.
   Weight: 1

#### Bonus points

- A second optional task completed.
- Clear evidence that the declined card (`4000 0000 0000 0002`) was handled gracefully, with nothing marked paid, alongside the successful purchase.
- The production-setup optional task delivered: separate development and production databases.

## Submission

Read an [in-depth guide about reviews here](https://doku.turingcollege.com/p/0771306d-bc1e-4b00-9153-c63adeb63a85).

#### Submission and scheduling a project review

To submit the project and allow the reviewer to view your work beforehand, use the `GitHub` repository that has been created for you. Please go through these materials to learn more about submitting projects, scheduling project reviews, and using `GitHub`:

- [Completing a Sprint, Submitting a Project and Scheduling Reviews](https://doku-v02-production.up.railway.app/p/f3dbf8bc-2dae-4230-938d-3144110ea74a)
- [Git and GitHub for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk)

Hand in the following before your 1-1 review call:

- **Your Turing College `GitHub` repository URL.**
- **The live URL of your deployed shop.** Your reviewer will open it before the call.
- **`README.md`** covering: what the shop sells; how the owner edits content through the admin panel; how to run it locally, including which environment variables to set and where the values come from (without pasting any secret); and which optional task you chose.
